fixes.explanation: Light it is, friend. The Teacher says "…wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). He looks at both and says wisdom wins. It's plain as turning on the kitchen light and seeing where the cookie sheet actually is.

Close, but the Teacher says the opposite here. He says the wise man has eyes in his head and the fool walks in darkness, "Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both." (Ecclesiastes 2:14). One fate, not two. That's the turn in the verse.

You'd think a wise man would just study harder, wouldn't you? But that's not what he asks. He says, "What then have I gained by being wise?" (Ecclesiastes 2:15). His question is about what the wisdom he already has has done for him.

Praise would be nice, but that's not what the Teacher says. He says "…there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come." (Ecclesiastes 2:16). The word he uses is forgotten, not praised.
He did, friend. The Teacher says plainly, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). That's a heavy thing to say. I think he really means it.

Loving life even more is a hopeful guess, but the Teacher goes the other direction. He says, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). Seeing that the wise and the fool both die and are forgotten (Ecclesiastes 2:16) is what comes right before it.

No battle in this verse, baker. The Teacher's reason is quieter: "…I must leave it to the man who comes after me." (Ecclesiastes 2:18). Battle never comes up. The reason he gives is that he must leave it.

False is right, baker. The Teacher says, "…my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 2:20). Despair, not peace. A few verses later he says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24).

Evil, friend. When a man who labored with wisdom, knowledge and skill must give his portion to one who hasn't worked for it, the Teacher says "…this too is futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). Those are his exact words. I think that one stings.
Mind it is, baker. The Teacher says, "even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Night comes and the thoughts keep right on going. That's one busy mind.

Gathering more isn't what he calls better, baker. What he says is better is this: "…to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Enjoying the work is the answer he gives. Piling up more isn't.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God." (Ecclesiastes 2:26). The sinner gathers, and the one who pleases God receives it. The verse closes by calling this "…futile and a pursuit of the wind."
